records.name_note: Sources split on which name leads. NC State's Common Name(s) list has exactly two entries -- "American Bladdernut" and "Bladdernut" -- in the same order as the page-title parenthetical "(American Bladdernut, Bladdernut)", and NC State's own body prose leads with "American bladdernut, is a fast-growing, upright, deciduous, perennial, flowering shrub or small tree...", so this NC State list is a lead. RHS's browser page title reads "Staphylea trifolia | American bladdernut", and the plant-profile subtitle rendered beneath the H1 "Staphylea trifolia" reads "American bladdernut" on its own, with "Other common names" listing only "American bladdernut". MoBot's displayed Common Name field, by contrast, carries the single value "bladdernut" (not "American bladdernut") for this species; a two-entry list sits behind a popup whose text exists only in the link's markup, and its rendered bullets read "bladdernut" and "American bladdernut" -- both names appear there but "bladdernut" is the field's displayed lead value. Two of the three dedicated single-species pages (NC State and RHS) lead with "American Bladdernut", so that name is used as common_name here.
unknowns: No admissible source found any toxicity/poison information for Staphylea trifolia -- NC State's Plant Type list carries no 'Poisonous' tag and its Problems module ('No serious insect or disease problems.' per MoBot; NC State shows the plant is resistant to honey fungus) carries no poison-related tags, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than guessed.

water_regime left null: NC State's body prose describes the plant growing 'in average, dry to medium, well-drained soils' and MoBot's structured Water field reads 'Dry to medium' -- both are ranges/mid-scale descriptions rather than a clean directive mapping to one of the four enum watering regimes, so no value was assigned; this is disclosed as a genus/species watering ambiguity rather than resolved by guessing.

full_shade is included in outdoor_sun_exposure based on NC State's own unconditional body prose ('...in part shade to full shade') and MoBot's structured Sun field ('Part shade to full shade'), even though NC State's structured Light field itself lists only Full sun and Partial Shade (not Full/Deep Shade) and RHS's Position field lists only Full sun and Partial shade -- disclosing that the structured Light/Position fields alone would not have supported full_shade.

day/night temperature fields, humidity fields, light_fc fields, chill_damage_f, fertilize fields, and water day-interval/dry-down fields are all left null: no admissible source frames Staphylea trifolia care in these terms (it is an in-ground, cold-hardy (USDA zones 3-8) native shrub/tree, not a container/houseplant subject with a stated fertilizer schedule or an explicit chill-damage onset temperature).

soil_ph_min/max left null per the pH rule: NC State lists no Soil pH field for this species, and RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', i.e. it explicitly admits both acid and alkaline soils, so neither a floor nor a ceiling is set.

records.name_note: All three admissible sources have dedicated single-species pages and all three lead with hop tree. NC State's Common Name(s) field lists Hoptree, Hop-tree, Stinking Ash, Wafer-ash, in the same order as the page-title parenthetical, and its Description opens 'Hoptree is a deciduous small tree or large shrub in the Rutaceae (citrus) family native to North Carolina.' MoBot's Common Name field carries the single value 'hop tree' and its Noteworthy Characteristics opens 'Ptelea trifoliata, commonly called hop tree...'; a later sentence in that paragraph lists three descriptive names — (a) hop tree, (b) wafer ash, (c) stinking ash. A longer common-name list sits behind a MoBot popup whose text exists only in the link's markup, so it is not quoted here. RHS's H1 is the botanical name alone with 'hop tree' as the plant-profile subtitle, and lists shrubby trefoil, stinking ash, swamp devil's bit, swamp dogwood, wafer ash, water ash, wing seed under Other common names. The lead is therefore 'Hoptree'/'hop tree.' Despite carrying 'ash' in several of its names, this species is not a true ash: NC State places it in 'the Rutaceae (citrus) family' and MoBot's Family field reads 'Rutaceae', whereas Fraxinus is not a Rutaceae genus. 'Common Hoptree' is not led by any admissible source's dedicated straight-species page (see unknowns).
records.toxicity_detail: NC State carries no structured Poison Part / Poison Severity / Poison Symptoms / Poison Toxic Principle block for this species — no such fields render on its page. Its Problems field carries the single entry 'Malodorous,' and its Tags list separately carries both '#malodorous' and '#contact dermatitis' — the latter indicating a skin-irritant hazard on contact, with no severity rating, symptom list, toxic principle, or animal scope given. The parts implicated in the odor are named by both North American sources: NC State says 'stinking ash comes from the malodorous fragrance of the flowers as well as bruised leaves and stems' and describes the leaf as 'malodorous when crushed' and the stems as 'pungent'; MoBot cites 'the unpleasant smell of not only the flowers but also bruised foliage and bark.' No Problem for Dogs, Problem for Cats, or Poisonous to Humans tag appears anywhere on the NC State page. RHS's dedicated page carries no Toxicity, skin-irritant, or harmful-if-eaten field at all, and MoBot's Problems paragraph is horticultural only ('No serious insect or disease problems. Some susceptibility to leaf spots.'). No admissible source scopes any toxicity or dermatitis claim to cats or dogs for this species, and the sources do not disagree on scope or edibility — none addresses either.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source scopes a toxicity claim to cats or dogs specifically for Ptelea trifoliata; the only hazard language found (NC State's 'Malodorous' Problems tag and its separate 'contact dermatitis' tag) names no animal at all, and RHS's dedicated page for this species has no Toxicity field whatsoever.

water_regime left null: NC State's Water Requirements field is 'Not specified,' and MoBot's structured Water field reads 'Dry to medium' — a mid/dry-scale reading that does not map cleanly onto keep_moist, keep_barely_moist, dry_surface_between, or dry_thoroughly_between. No species-specific watering statement (as opposed to a bare structured field) was found on any admissible source.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: RHS's Soil pH field lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' as acceptable — i.e., both acid and alkaline soils are listed as acceptable — so neither a floor nor a ceiling is set. NC State's Soil pH field is 'Not specified.'
fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength left null: no admissible source discusses a fertilizing schedule, dilution strength, or active months for this species.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, direct_sun_hours_max, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis all left null: no admissible source gives species-specific figures for these; only hardiness-zone ranges are given (NC State 3a–9b; MoBot Zone 4–9; RHS H6), which are zone/survival ratings, not onset temperatures, humidity levels, or light-intensity figures, and this is an in-ground landscape tree/shrub rather than a container plant framed around dry-down or day-interval watering.

'Common Hoptree' — one of the four common names sometimes associated with this species — is not led by any admissible source's dedicated straight-species page. UF/IFAS (edis.ifas.ufl.edu / ask.ifas.ufl.edu) carries only cultivar-specific pages for 'Aurea' and 'Glauca' (excluded here as cultivar pages per instructions), and its straight-species fact sheet (Fact Sheet ST-530) is hosted only at hort.ifas.ufl.edu, which is not on the admissible domain list.

No dedicated species page for Ptelea trifoliata was found on hgic.clemson.edu, extension.umd.edu, or fieldreport.caes.uga.edu. A Penn State Extension Master Gardener teaching-garden listing page mentions 'Wafer ash' among its plantings but is a garden inventory page, not a species care page, so it was not used as a source here.

full_sun is carried in outdoor_sun_exposure at landing on two of the three structured sun fields -- NC State's Light field (Deep shade, Full sun, Partial Shade) and RHS's Position field (Full sun, Partial shade) -- while MoBot's structured Sun field reads 'Part shade to full shade' and its Culture text adds only 'Tolerates full sun.'; MoBot's omission is disclosed here rather than used to drop a value two sources list plainly. No species-specific scorch or avoid-sun warning was found in any source.

records.name_note: Sources differ in how they present common names. NC State's Common Name(s) field lists five entries alphabetically — American Ash, Canadian Ash, Green Ash, Red Ash, Water Ash — in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, while NC State's own Description prose opens 'Green ash is a native, medium-sized, broadleaf, deciduous tree in the olive family (Oleaceae).' NC State additionally serves a page for each of those five names under this same record, including 'Green Ash - Fraxinus pennsylvanica,' so the alias pages are not a taxonomic split. RHS's H1 is the bare binomial, with 'green ash' rendered as the plant-profile subtitle and in the page title 'Fraxinus pennsylvanica | green ash'; its separate Other common names field reads 'American ash, Canadian ash, red American ash, red ash, white ash.' MoBot's rendered Common Name field shows the single value 'green ash'; its longer Common Names list exists only inside the popup link's markup and is therefore not quoted here. MoBot's dedicated single-species page, RHS's subtitle and title, and NC State's body prose all converge on 'green ash,' so Green Ash is used as the species-distinguishing common name. Two of the alternates, 'American Ash' and 'White Ash,' are the two names NC State assigns to the sibling species Fraxinus americana, a further reason not to use them here.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: none of the admissible sources fetched for this species (NC State Extension Plant Toolbox, Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder, RHS) carry a Poison block, a Poisonous Plant Type tag, or any cat/dog-scoped toxicity statement for Fraxinus pennsylvanica -- NC State's page has no Poison Severity/Symptoms/Toxic Principle/Part fields and no 'Poisonous' tag in its Plant Type list.

Emerald ash borer susceptibility and the resulting 'no longer recommended for planting' guidance (stated identically on NC State and MoBot) is a pest/disease problem statement, not a care value, and is deliberately excluded from any care field per task instructions.

soil_ph_min left null: NC State's Soil pH field shows a closed Neutral (6.0-8.0) band plus an open-ended Acid (<6.0) band, so no floor can be set; the RHS species page for this species carries no cultivation/pH section to cross-check against, so per rule 6 the floor is left null and disclosed rather than assumed.

The RHS species page (rhs.org.uk/plants/7320/fraxinus-pennsylvanica/details) was confirmed by both URL slug and page title ('Fraxinus pennsylvanica | green ash') to be this species, but unlike RHS cultivar pages it carries no cultivation/growing-conditions section (no Position, Soil, pH, Hardiness, or Ultimate height fields) -- only Botanical Details (Family, Native to GB/Ireland, Genus, Name Status, Plant Range) and Other common names/Synonyms. This is why no soil/light/hardiness data was drawn from RHS for this species.

No admissible-source content found distinguishing Green Ash from Red Ash as separate taxa for care purposes -- NC State treats 'Red Ash' and 'Water Ash' as auto-generated alias pages of this same Fraxinus pennsylvanica record, not a split species, so no Red-Ash-specific values were sought or included.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on lead name. NC State's Common Name(s) field lists seven entries alphabetically — Black Locust, Common Locust, False Acacia, Green Locust, Pea Flower Locust, White Locust, Yellow Locust — the same order as the parenthetical in its page title, with Black Locust first in both. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page for this species gives 'Common Name: black locust'. RHS instead titles its profile 'Robinia pseudoacacia | false acacia' and lists black locust among its Other common names. common_name follows the two North American sources, which both lead with Black Locust.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block (human-scoped) rates Poison Severity as High. Poison Symptoms: "If ingested, it may cause death in humans and livestock and pets. Depression, weakness, dilated pupils, vomiting, bloody diarrhea, weak pulse, coldness of arms and legs, paleness, and shock." Poison Toxic Principle: Robin, a phytotoxin; robitin, a glycoside; robinine, an alkaloid. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Bark, Leaves, Seeds. NC State's Plant Type field flags the species as Poisonous (Plant Type: Native Plant, Poisonous, Tree, Woody Plant), and its structured Problems field lists five values: Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. The Problem-for-Cats and Problem-for-Dogs values are what scope the risk to cats and dogs specifically; the Poison block above is headed 'Poisonous to Humans', though its symptom text itself states ingestion 'may cause death in humans and livestock and pets'. Separately, this tree is armed: NC State's Appendage field reads 'Spines, Thorns' and its Stem Description states, 'Its branches are usually armed with short, paired spines (to 1.25 inches long) adjacent to each leaf scar.'
unknowns: soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists all three bands as open-ended (Acid <6.0, Neutral 6.0-8.0, Alkaline >8.0), and RHS's Soil pH field independently lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' as all acceptable, so no floor or ceiling can be set in either direction.

records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads. NC State's Common Name(s) field is a four-entry alphabetized stacked list (Grey Elm, Red Elm, Slippery Elm, Soft Elm) whose order matches the page-title parenthetical, so its leading entry is Grey Elm; NC State's body prose, however, opens 'Slippery Elm is a long-lived elm tree...'. MoBot's single Common Name field reads 'slippery elm.' RHS's page title and plant-profile subtitle are 'moose elm,' with an Other common names field reading 'moose elm, red elm, slippery elm.' Of the three dedicated single-species pages, only MoBot leads with 'slippery elm'; it is used here because it is the one name that appears on all three pages and NC State's own prose adopts it, with RHS's 'moose elm' and NC State's leading 'Grey Elm' disclosed as the dissenting leads.
unknowns: No admissible source discusses toxicity to cats or dogs for Ulmus rubra (NC State carries no Poison Information field for this species at all); toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than guessed.

NC State's Soil pH field lists all three bands — Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0), and Alkaline (>8.0) — as acceptable, i.e. open-ended on both ends, so no numeric soil_ph_min or soil_ph_max can be derived; RHS's page for this species carries no pH field to check against.

MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium' field is mid-scale and, per instructions, cannot support a keep_moist water_regime; no species-specific watering statement was found in any admissible source, so water_regime is left null. This is a disclosed conflict/absence, not a resolved value.

No admissible source gives numeric light (foot-candle) values or a species-specific direct-sun-hour statement for Ulmus rubra; NC State's Light field is categorical only (Full sun / Partial Shade), so light_fc_min, light_fc_good, and direct_sun_hours_max are left null.
No admissible source gives a humidity requirement, a chill-damage onset temperature, day/night temperature ranges, or a fertilizing schedule/strength for this species; all such fields are left null.

RHS's dedicated Ulmus rubra page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/161727/ulmus-rubra/details) carries no Position, Soil, or pH fields — only Botanical Details (Family, Genus description, Name Status) and Other common names/Synonyms — so it could not corroborate or contradict NC State's structured sun, soil, or drainage fields.
Dutch elm disease and phloem necrosis are documented by NC State and MoBot as disease problems for this species, not care values, and were excluded from the schema per task instructions.
MoBot's Culture prose (inner bark, medicinal Native American use) was treated as historical/description content rather than care data and was not used to populate any field.

Clemson (hgic.clemson.edu), UF/IFAS (edis.ifas.ufl.edu / ask.ifas.ufl.edu), Penn State (extension.psu.edu), University of Maryland (extension.umd.edu), and UGA (fieldreport.caes.uga.edu) were searched but no dedicated single-species Ulmus rubra page was found on any of them; only NC State, MoBot, and RHS yielded admissible content for this species.

part_shade was excluded from outdoor_sun_exposure at landing: NC State's Light field does carry 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', but MoBot's structured Sun field reads 'Full sun' alone and every shade statement on either page is a tolerance clause -- MoBot 'Tolerant of light shade.' and NC State 'It will tolerate drought and part shade but prefers sun and moist loam or clay loam soils.' -- so the single structured tag is disclosed here rather than carried.

records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) field lists three entries alphabetically - Common Mulberry, Mulberry, Red Mulberry - the same order as the page title's parenthetical; its body prose calls the species "Red Mulberry." UF/IFAS FR326, a standalone publication on this species alone, has a Common Name heading reading "Red Mulberry." MoBot's Common Name field carries a single value, "Common Name: red mulberry." RHS's page title and plant-profile subtitle read "red mulberry," with "American mulberry" listed separately under Other common names. UF/IFAS, MoBot and RHS each lead with Red Mulberry; NC State's list leads with Common Mulberry, but its own prose for this species uses Red Mulberry.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State carries a human-scoped Poison block for this species: Poison Severity is "Low"; Poison Symptoms reads "Causes low toxicity if eaten.  Hallucinations and stomach upset from unripe fruit and sap."; Poison Toxic Principle is "Unidentified"; Causes Contact Dermatitis is "Yes"; and the full Poison Part list is "Sap/Juice." The same page co-lists "Poisonous" beside "Edible" in its Plant Type field and carries both a "#poisonous" and an "#edible fruits" tag, and its Problems field carries "Poisonous to Humans." Its body prose states that the fruit, "if eaten when unripe, are poisonous as is the milky white sap that all parts of the tree produces," while "Fruits that are eaten when ripe are harmless." UF/IFAS FR326 separately warns that "Male trees are extremely allergenic and should be avoided, while female trees cause few or no allergies," and that "The pollen from members of the Morus genus can cause allergies ranging from hay fever to asthma." This Poison block and its severity rating are human-scoped (from NC State's "Poisonous to Humans" heading); NC State's own structured tags separately mark the species "#non-toxic for cats" and "#non-toxic for dogs" (also "#non-toxic for horses"), so the poisoning risk described here is not carried over to cats or dogs.
unknowns: chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, direct_sun_hours_max, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null because no admissible source states species-specific values for Morus rubra for these fields (NC State's Light field legend gives only a generic site-wide hour range, not species-specific prose, so it was not used for direct_sun_hours_max).

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null: NC State's page for Morus rubra carries no Soil pH field at all, and RHS's pH field lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' with both extremes explicitly acceptable, so neither a floor nor a ceiling is supported.

water_regime is left null: no admissible source frames an explicit watering statement for this species. MoBot's structured Water field reads 'Medium' (mid-scale), which per the schema rule is disclosed only as a counterpoint and cannot support keep_moist; NC State's and MoBot's cultivation prose describe rich, moist, well-drained soil, which is a soil descriptor rather than a watering instruction.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are left null: this is an in-ground landscape tree and no admissible source frames watering in dry-down or day-interval terms for it.

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes full_shade: NC State's structured Light field lists 'Deep shade' alongside Full sun and Partial Shade, but MoBot's structured Sun field ('Full sun to part shade') excludes deep shade, and NC State's own body prose narrows cultivation to 'full sun to part shade.' Per the rule that a shade value present in only one of the two North American structured fields is disclosed rather than carried, deep/full shade is disclosed here but not included in the list.

is_houseplant is inferred as false from NC State's Plant Type field ('Tree') and its 25-60 ft mature landscape height in USDA zones 4a-9b; no admissible source explicitly frames this species as a houseplant or explicitly rules it out.

toxic_to_pets is set to false based on NC State's own tags '#non-toxic for cats' and '#non-toxic for dogs', which directly and separately name both animals covered by this field; this coexists with NC State's human-scoped Poison block covering unripe fruit and the plant's milky sap.

Clemson HGIC's 'Red vs. White Mulberry (Morus rubra vs. Morus alba)' page (an admissible-domain comparison page) could not be retrieved — it returned a Cloudflare bot-challenge page rather than content — so no Clemson-sourced material is included in this record.

Ripe-fruit edibility is stated only as: NC State's Edibility field says ripe fruits are sweet, juicy, and can be eaten raw or made into pies, jellies, jams, breads, muffins, and cakes, and its body prose says fruit eaten when ripe is harmless; no broader edibility claim is made beyond that.

normalizations: 2026-09-05: forty-eighth batch (cruise throttle) -- a fourth native tree set: American Bladdernut, Hoptree, Green Ash, Black Locust, Slippery Elm, and Red Mulberry. Clean first run (12/12 agents, 1.28M subagent tokens). land_check.py and covered.py ran clean; verify_quotes.py 88/94 reachable quotes before repair, the six MISSes all fixed here: four abbreviated NC State Light strings ('Full sun (6+ hours)', 'Partial Shade (2-6 hours)', a bare three-word list) replaced by the rendered values, Slippery Elm's soil_base citation -- a semicolon-joined synthesis attributed to a 'Habitat' field the page does not have -- replaced by the real Landscape Location values, and Hoptree's confused-with citation dropped with its sub-claim. Sun values: Black Locust and Slippery Elm drop part_shade (single NC State tags against MoBot's and RHS's full-sun-only structured fields, with MoBot's 'avoid shady locations' and both sources' tolerance clauses), while Hoptree carries full_sun on NC State's Light field plus RHS's Position field with MoBot's omission disclosed. Four nulled citation-form fields were restored with values unchanged: Green Ash's scientific_name_accepted (RHS H1 paired with the Name Status value) and soil_base (uncited; now on NC State's Soil Texture and MoBot's Suggested Use), Black Locust's and Slippery Elm's is_houseplant (a Plant Type list missing Woody Plant; a label carrying a synthesized siting string), and Slippery Elm's soil_base. Every name_note was replaced with the auditor's corrected wording (invented 'N entries marks no primary' conventions, overstated leads, RHS title strings called subtitles, a look-alike module read as taxonomy); three toxicity_detail fields were repaired as trimmed safety fields with the auditor's verbatim additions -- Black Locust's spines and its full Problems and Plant Type fields, Red Mulberry's Poisonous-beside-Edible plant type, its whole-tree sap clause and UF/IFAS's pollen allergen warning, Hoptree's odor-bearing parts and #malodorous tag -- and Black Locust's original recital was recovered from the research agent's journal output. toxic_to_pets=true on Black Locust rests on NC State's cat and dog tags (children and horses disclosed); Red Mulberry is false on explicit non-toxic-for-cats/dogs tags; the other four are null (no cat/dog-scoped source).
